keyVerseText: I have sewed sackcloth upon my skin, and defiled my horn in the dust.
rootMeaning: The Hebrew noun גֶּלֶד (geled) is derived from an unused root likely meaning 'to polish,' which suggests a focus on the smooth, outward surface of something. This etymology enriches the common English gloss 'skin' by emphasizing not just the skin as a covering, but as a polished, visible layer that can reflect condition or experience. Thus, geled points to the human skin as a tangible and sensitive boundary between the inner person and the external world.
usageInScripture: The word גֶּלֶד (geled) appears only once in the entire Hebrew Bible, specifically in Job 16:15, where it is translated as 'upon my skin.' This singular usage highlights the intimate and personal nature of the term, consistently referring to human skin as a physical and symbolic element. The limited occurrence underscores its precise and poignant application rather than a broad or varied semantic range.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding גֶּלֶד (geled) as 'skin' with the nuance of a polished, exposed surface invites believers to consider the vulnerability and humanity of the biblical figures who suffer and express pain. The skin is not merely a biological covering but a witness to affliction and endurance, reminding us of Christ's own incarnation and suffering in human flesh. This word deepens our appreciation for the incarnational reality of Jesus, who took on human skin to redeem fallen humanity, and it calls believers to recognize the sacredness of the human body as part of God's creation and redemptive plan.
keyVerseReflection: In Job 16:15, the phrase 'I have sewed sackcloth upon my skin' uses גֶּלֶד (geled) to convey the personal and physical extent of Job's mourning and distress. The skin, as the immediate covering of the body, emphasizes how deeply Job's grief penetrates—not only his spirit but his very flesh. This vivid imagery of sackcloth against the skin powerfully communicates the totality of his suffering and humility before God.
